## **Executive Summary**

The most critical component of any environmental assessment (EA) is the evaluation of a project’s effects on the environment. As defined by the _Canadian Environmental Assessment Act_ , the environment includes all components of the Earth, including land, water, air, all organic and inorganic matter and living organisms, and the interacting natural systems involving any of the above. Although every EA should consider the potential for affecting all components of the environment, this document has a much narrower focus, providing guidance for assessing the potential effects of wind energy projects on bird populations.

As the demand for clean energy increases, wind energy generating stations are being constructed across Canada. Wind has been used successfully across the globe to generate electricity, and is generally considered to be an environmentally healthy and viable means of meeting part of our energy demands. However, concerns have been raised about the possible impact of wind turbines on bird populations.  These concerns were first raised in the 1980s when it was discovered that large numbers of raptors were colliding with wind turbines and their associated power lines in the Altamont Pass and Tehachapi Pass Wind Resource Areas in California. Despite the unique combination of site specific factors that contribute to the unacceptable effect on the area’s hawks and eagles, the public’s perceptions have created a mistrust of all wind power projects, which has rippled across North America **.** As a result, proposals for wind energy projects throughout the United States and Canada have often been accompanied by concerns, scepticism and calls for cautious advancement of the technology and development of wind energy facilities, regardless of a site’s attributes with respect to bird populations, scale of facility or siting.

In Canada, the United States, and elsewhere in the world, a considerable amount of research has been undertaken in assessing the effect of wind turbines on bird populations. In almost all cases, the effect of collision or disturbance on bird populations was minimal. However, any human structure can have an adverse effect on the environment, and the likelihood of this effect and its significance is greater if the structure is not properly sited. Appropriate site selection appears to be the key factor in preventing potential significant negative impacts on birds. Although there is still much to be learned (especially offshore, in maritime areas, the far north and other habitats that have not yet had wind turbines situated and sufficiently studied), there is sufficient information currently available that provides general trends which will assist in preventing the problems that have occurred at some wind energy sites.

Raptors are often cited as the bird group most threatened by wind facilities because of the fatalities that continue to occur at Altamont Pass, but it has been found that in almost all  areas, raptors are able to avoid wind turbines, resulting in very few or no collisions. A number of factors contribute to these deaths in California, including unusually high raptor densities, topography and possibly older technology. Awareness of these factors and how they relate to proposed wind energy facilities in Canada should lead to a reduction in raptor mortality attributed to wind turbines.

In North America, the birds most commonly observed to collide with wind turbines are songbirds. Often, these collisions are believed to occur at night during nocturnal migration, although collisions also occur during the day. Factors such as topography, turbine lighting and numbers of birds moving through an area on migration can influence the number of collisions observed at a facility,

although it is apparent that the operation of the turbines is less important than the lighting and height of the structure and presence of guy wires in contributing to collision risk. An assessment of these factors during the EA, coupled with pre-construction and post-construction surveys, will help to mitigate potential problems with respect to avian collision with wind farm structures.

It is possible that the greatest adverse effect that wind energy facilities may have on birds is disturbance to breeding and wintering birds (except in areas where poor habitat quality exists, such as agricultural and industrial areas). Unfortunately, this is the least studied impact of wind energy facilities on birds. Nevertheless, the potential for disturbance effects on breeding and wintering birds should be considered at all sites. This is especially important in areas where Species at Risk are present as part of the breeding or wintering bird community, in prairie habitat where certain susceptible bird species (e.g., Sharp-tailed Grouse, Sage Grouse) are found breeding, and in offshore areas that are important feeding areas or movement corridors.

Recently, there has been much interest in placing wind energy facilities offshore. Although none have yet been built in North America, several exist in Europe. It has been difficult to assess mortality at offshore locations due to the victims falling into the water. Hopefully, with recent improvements in video surveillance, this unknown can be resolved. What has been determined is that certain species avoid turbines and rows of turbines may act as barriers to movement. Wind farms may also displace birds from foraging areas. There is still much that needs to be learned about the effect of offshore facilities on bird populations, and proposed projects in Canada should proceed cautiously. Turbines may cause barriers to movement, may change the distribution of forage species, and may disturb breeding, wintering or staging waterfowl and waterbirds. Detailed preconstruction studies should help identify potential problems and how they may be mitigated before a project is constructed.

The problems that have occurred at some sites need not be duplicated, as the mistakes of the past have provided information that can be used to site wind turbines in such a way as to minimise the effect on bird populations. A precautionary approach, however, is needed at this stage, since the majority of the research that is available has been done in Europe and in western and mid-western North America. Canada is a very large and diverse country with many landforms and habitats that are significantly different from the areas studied. This makes the collection of pre- and postconstruction monitoring important at sites across Canada. Until further research is done in this country, it will be unknown if other habitats or other features may cause significant numbers of collisions or unacceptable disturbance effects. It is for this reason that this is a ‘living document’ that will be updated to reflect information gathered in this country and elsewhere in the world.

To help reduce the impact on birds, it is important that proper evaluations of the potential impact projects may cause to an area’s bird population are conducted. Projects should be assessed on a site by site basis, considering a number of factors that may increase risk to bird populations. The presence of large numbers of birds passing through an area alone should not prevent a project from progressing, but will require a greater amount of pre-construction monitoring and research to determine if there are other factors such as landforms, habitat features and bird behaviours that increase collision risk and make the site unsuitable for development. Where there is potential for disturbance ( _e_ . _g_ ., near colonial nesting seabird colonies or foraging areas), Environment Canada may request additional studies to be completed before a site is deemed acceptable.

In areas where sufficient information (available through consultation and literature review) indicates or predicts a low risk to birds (generally urbanized areas and intensive agricultural sites where there are no other features present that would increase collision risk or disturbance), the project can proceed with little or no pre-construction monitoring.

## **1. Introduction**

Environmental guidelines for wind energy projects have been created, or are being developed, for many countries, including the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom. In response to Canada’s developing wind industry, Environment Canada has produced Environmental Assessment (EA) guidelines that help to address a specific concern of regulators and the public: the effect of wind energy projects on birds. One of Environment Canada’s goals is the protection of migratory birds and it is for this reason that these specific guidelines have been produced.

This document provides guidelines for assessing the environmental effects of wind energy facilities on birds in Canada, and has three main purposes. Firstly, it provides proponents, regulatory agencies, and the public with valuable background information on bird-wind turbine interactions from around the world that may be used to better assess the potential effects of wind energy projects on birds. Secondly, this document identifies the types of information Environment Canada expects in EAs for wind energy projects. Thirdly, it outlines a standardised monitoring approach to facilitate information gathering and sharing across Canada that would be useful for both pre-construction impact assessment and post-construction environmental effects monitoring. It is expected that information gathered using these suggested approaches, or similar methods, may be used to better identify and mitigate negative effects for future wind energy projects.

This document is predominantly conceptual in its approach, with an emphasis on providing guiding principles rather than a detailed checklist of information that is required for an EA report. Although these guidelines focus on birds, the group of animals which has attracted the most attention over the last decade, Environment Canada recognises that other wildlife may be adversely affected by wind energy developments. For example, some studies have reported bat mortality due to collision with wind turbines (Erickson _et al._ 2002), but little information is presently known regarding the extent of impact, the reasons why and/or how bats are being killed or even the incidence of bat-turbine interactions. Other wildlife species may be identified as Valued Ecosystem Components (VECs) for particular wind energy projects, and impacts should be assessed by the proponent on a case by case basis.

Environment Canada recognises that some components of these guidelines may not be applicable to all projects, and that the scale of an assessment should reflect the scale of the project and sitespecific issues. It should also be noted that wind energy in Canada is still in its relative infancy. As more projects are constructed and bird interactions are monitored across the country, new information will become available and should be considered when environmental assessments and impact statements are undertaken. These guidelines should not be regarded as either exhaustive or restrictive, but should be thought to be a “living” document. As such, these guidelines will not preclude requests by Environment Canada (or any other regulatory agency) for additional information in relation to a particular project. It should also be noted that these guidelines may be updated periodically as new information becomes available and that new versions will be made available on the Environment Canada website (http:\\www.ec.gc.ca\).

Successful wind energy projects exist across the globe, including facilities in Africa, Asia, Europe,

Australia, South America, the U.S. and Canada. However, concerns have been raised by the public and regulators regarding the potential environmental impact of these facilities and in particular their potential impacts on birds. This issue first became apparent in the late 1980s when birds of prey, especially Red-tailed Hawks, American Kestrels and Golden Eagles were first noticed to be killed by wind turbines and their associated power lines at Altamont Pass and Tehachapi Pass, in California. The high numbers of raptors killed at these sites have proven to be more of an anomaly than a typical situation. Nevertheless, these well-known examples continue to spark concerns among the public and other organisations and, more than anything else, have generated widespread fears that turbines are invariably lethal to birds. As the industry matures and expands across Canada, it becomes vitally important that EAs of proposed wind energy projects be undertaken, considering the existing conditions of each site, and information from other studies that have examined the post-construction effects of wind energy facilities.

As the reader will see in Chapter 2, the observed effects of wind energy projects on bird populations are to-date generally small. Observed effects can be broken down into two basic groups: direct fatality and injury through collisions with wind farm structures, and indirect effects through disturbance and habitat loss. Most empirical data on the effects of wind energy facilities on birds comes from U.S. and European research. In the U.S.A., most of the work has concentrated on assessing and documenting bird collisions with wind turbines, whereas research in Europe has placed more focus on examining indirect effects such as disturbance. Most of the research on wind power and birds has not been published in peer reviewed journals. Instead, studies are primarily industry funded and reported on-line, which has advantages and disadvantages. It is advantageous that information from these studies can be quickly obtained by anyone on-line, without the long lag time of peer-reviewed journals. Readers can also assess for themselves whether the studies are valid and have been conducted in an appropriate manner. However, the fact that most of the studies are industry-funded and presented without a formal peer review causes scepticism and criticism among opponents of wind farms.

Most wind energy facilities are located in areas where the wind resource is plentiful. In Canada, suitable areas tend to occur offshore or onshore in coastal areas, on ridges and mountains, in open agricultural areas and other open habitats. Many of these areas contain sensitive habitats and/or bird species, which heighten the importance of assessing the effects of wind energy projects. With this in mind, and Environment Canada’s goal to conserve migratory birds, these guidelines are aimed at helping proponents provide information in EA documentation with an appropriate level of detail. Additionally, this document will also provide proponents with a framework that may be used to show due diligence in trying to eliminate the risk of bird fatalities. This is especially important given that federal regulations under the _Migratory Birds Convention Act_ (MBCA) and _Species at Risk Act_ (SARA) prohibit the disturbance or killing of protected birds, while in some provinces provincial regulations provide additional protection to birds and other wildlife. Refer to the appropriate **provincial** natural resource agency for further information on wildlife legislation.

Environment Canada recognises that relative to wind energy facilities, there are other more important (e.g., tall buildings, transmission towers) causes of bird death and habitat destruction, but wishes to address potential issues caused by wind energy projects while the Canadian wind energy industry is still relatively small.  In addition, public perceptions that wind turbines automatically

pose significant threats to birds also need to be addressed. By having proponents follow these guidelines and by taking an adaptive approach that incorporates the most recent and comprehensive information, Environment Canada’s goal is to ensure that conservation and protection of migratory bird populations as well as Species at Risk is achieved.

There is much more to learn about bird and wind turbine interactions and a precautionary approach is required to assess impacts of wind energy facilities on bird populations. Technology is advancing quickly, and potential environmental effects seen in earlier studies may be avoided with proper siting of facilities and newer turbine and facility designs. It is imperative that assessments be done with an understanding of the most current information based on the appropriate technology. The adaptive approach Environment Canada is advocating with these guidelines will allow the sharing of the most current and relevant information, including mitigation measures and other aspects of impact management. The co-operation of proponents with Environment Canada in this regard will allow for efficient management of resources and a refinement of best practices that will only benefit the industry and advocates of bird conservation.

This document is structured to help proponents assess the effects of wind energy projects on birds. Chapter 2 provides background to wind energy in Canada and internationally, and identifies the reasons why these guidelines have been produced. Chapter 3 provides details of studies examining the effects of wind energy projects on birds, including both direct and indirect effects. This literature review is organised taxonomically, allowing the reader to gain an understanding of what issues may be encountered for each group of birds. Chapter 4 highlights specific design issues that have been identified during other studies of wind farms, and Chapter 5 discusses siting issues that should be considered during the planning of a wind farm. Chapter 6 presents information and guidance on the baseline data recommended for an EA. The amount of detail required for an EA will depend on the project’s size and the sensitivity of the proposed site. Table 2 within this chapter gives specific guidance as to the level of detail and amount of effort that is required for different projects. Collection of the baseline data should be planned with future monitoring needs in mind, and a protocol should be setup at this stage of the study, if appropriate. Once the baseline has been described, Chapters 4, 5 and 8 can be used to further plan the project. Chapter 7 provides a discussion on environmental effects monitoring and Chapter 8 presents some information on postconstruction mitigation measures. Finally, a list of cited references and a list of other useful references and resources that could be consulted for more detail are provided.

## **2. Background**

## **2.1 Green Power**

As demand for electricity increases and government efforts are directed toward reducing our impact on the environment, both within Canada and internationally, more Canadians are seeking sources of cleaner energy. To help consumers identify “green” electricity products, the "Guideline on Renewable Low-Impact Electricity" establishes criteria for the certification and licensing of facilities to produce renewable low-impact electricity under Environment Canada's Environmental Choice Program.

The Program's EcoLogo[TM] provides consumers with an easy means of identifying electricity products that put less stress on the environment. To receive the EcoLogo[TM] designation, a power generation facility must meet stringent environmental criteria and contribute to cleaner air and reduced greenhouse gases. Electricity distributors that comply with the guideline will be able to use the EcoLogo[TM] to market their electricity products encouraging a shift in the marketplace, from electricity generated by non-renewable and polluting sources (e.g., coal) to renewable low-impact sources.

All of the commonly used methods of power generation cause negative environmental effects, though some are worse than others. Nuclear power creates thermal pollution in waterbodies and causes concern over waste disposal issues and the potential for harming the environment with radiation. Large hydroelectric facilities disrupt aquatic ecosystems and may flood large areas of land, leading to various environmental concerns, including significant loss of bird habitat. However, adverse effects of coal-burning co-generation plants have caused the most concern among environmentalists, regulators and the general public. Coal’s contribution to greenhouse gas emissions and poor air quality has fuelled a need for alternative sources of energy. Climate change may have large impacts on natural habitats, and on birds that are dependent upon them. Harnessing wind energy is an affordable form of power generation that is pollution-free with relatively little environmental impact, advantages which have lead to a dramatic increase in its popularity in recent years. In evaluating the significance of impacts, it is important to consider the larger picture (less air pollution, fewer rivers dammed resulting in habitat loss, closing of coal-generated plants).

Several factors have led to the recent rise of wind energy across Canada and elsewhere in the World. The most significant factor has been a change in environmental awareness and an increase in concern over human and environmental health, as mentioned above. With such international endeavours as the Kyoto Protocol, alternative energy production has been pushed to the forefront in people’s minds. The Canadian government has recognised the importance of cleaner sources of energy in light of its commitment to the Kyoto Protocol, and has created the Wind Power Production Incentive (WPPI) program. Over the next several years (2002-2007), the WPPI program will provide financial support for the installation of 1,000 MW of power capacity, hoping to leverage $1.5 billion in capital investments across Canada. Participating energy producers will receive a financial incentive of approximately one cent per kWh during the first ten years of a wind farm’s operation. In addition, the Canadian Government has set a target that at least 10% of

Canada's new electricity generating capacity in 2010 should come from emerging renewable energy sources, including wind.

Although still more expensive than other traditional energy sources, the cost of wind energy has dropped considerably during the last decade. Continuing advances in technology have made wind energy generation more efficient and profitable, bringing the cost down from $0.30 per kWh to much more competitive rates. Investments in wind energy need not be as large as they were in the past, which is translating into lower electricity rates and, in turn, is encouraging consumers to switch to cleaner sources of energy. With the added incentive of the federal WPPI program, affordable and clean wind power generation will likely become a strong competitor in the electricity marketplace within the next decade.

## **2.2 Environment Canada’s Mandate**

Environment Canada's mandate is to preserve and enhance the quality of the natural environment, including water, air and soil quality; conserve Canada's renewable resources, including migratory birds and other flora and fauna; conserve and protect Canada's water resources; carry out meteorology; enforce the rules made by the Canada - United States International Joint Commission relating to boundary waters; and co-ordinate environmental policies and programs for the federal government.

Environment Canada's vision is to see a Canada where people make responsible decisions about the environment, and where the environment is thereby sustained for the benefit of present and future generations, and for the benefit of biotic and abiotic components in and for themselves.

Environment Canada's mission is to make sustainable development a reality in Canada by helping Canadians live and prosper in an environment that needs to be respected, protected and conserved.

Environment Canada has the responsibility to protect migratory birds and Species at Risk, and therefore must ensure that populations of migratory birds are not adversely affected by projects such as wind energy developments. As a Federal Authority under the _Canadian Environmental Assessment Act_ , Environment Canada also provides advice on migratory birds, Species at Risk and natural habitats, to other federal departments on private and public land. Environment Canada also supports the Government of Canada’s commitment to the Kyoto Protocol, and is committed to encouraging the establishment of alternative energy sources such as wind power.

## **2.3 Legislation, Policy and Initiatives**

Most birds residing in Canada do so for only part of the year, and are thus considered migratory. Most of these migratory species have been internationally protected under the _Migratory Birds Convention_ of 1916, implemented in Canada in 1917 through the _Migratory Birds Convention Act_ (MBCA). This act is the Canadian domestic legislation implementing the international treaty between Canada and the United States to protect migratory birds. The MBCA (paragraph 5)

prohibits any person to possess a migratory bird or nest, or buy, sell exchange or give a migratory bird or nest or make it the subject of a commercial transaction. The _Migratory Birds Regulations_ (MBR), in Section 6, prohibits the killing, disturbance, destruction, taking of a nest, egg, nest shelter, eider duck shelter or duck box of a migratory bird; or the possession of a live migratory bird, or its carcass, skin, nest or egg, except under authority of a permit. It is important to note that under the MBR, no permits can be issued for economic activities or development projects. Section 35 of the MBR also prohibits in general the deposit of harmful substances in any waters or any area frequented by migratory birds anywhere in Canada.

In 1996, federal, provincial and territorial governments endorsed the _Accord for the Protection of Species at Risk,_ and committed to a national approach to protect Species at Risk. Governments agreed to develop complementary legislation, regulations, policies and programs to identify and protect threatened and endangered species and their critical habitats. In June 2003, the _Species at Risk Act_ (SARA) was proclaimed.

SARA protects plants and animals listed in Schedule 1 of the Act (the List of Wildlife Species at Risk), and makes it an offence to kill, harm, harass, capture or take an individual of a listed endangered, threatened or extirpated species; possess, collect, buy, sell or trade an individual of a listed endangered, threatened or extirpated species, or its parts or derivatives; damage or destroy the residence of one or more individuals of a listed endangered or threatened species, or a listed extirpated species if a recovery strategy has recommended its reintroduction into the wild in Canada. These prohibitions apply to aquatic species and migratory birds covered by the _Migratory Birds Convention Act_ , 1994 wherever they are found and to all listed endangered, threatened or extirpated species on federal lands. For listed species located outside of federal lands, the provinces and territories are given the first opportunity to protect them through their laws. If those measures are not in place or are insufficient, the _Species at Risk Act_ has a "safety net" whereby certain prohibitions may apply by order of the Governor in Council. SARA also provides a way for the government to take immediate action to protect a wildlife species in an emergency.

SARA also requires that every person required by law to conduct a federal EA must (1) notify the competent minister(s) in the likelihood that a project will affect a listed wildlife species or its critical habitat; (2) identify the adverse effects of the project on the listed wildlife species; and, if the project is carried out, (3) ensure that measures are taken to avoid or lessen the effects and to monitor them. The measures must be taken in a way that is consistent with any applicable recovery strategy and action plans.

Besides the MBCA, MBR, SARA and _Canadian Environmental Assessment Act_ , other relevant legislation, policies and initiatives at the national level as well as the provincial/territorial level should be considered when assessing the effects of wind turbines on migratory birds (these need not have legal status but can act as a flag to the importance of the area to birds). It may include consideration of the following:

- _Canada Wildlife Act_

- _Oceans Act_

- Various provincial/territorial legislation (e.g., _Endangered Species Act_ s, _Fish and Wildlife Act_ s)

- The Federal Policy on Wetland Conservation

- Migratory Bird Sanctuary Regulations

- North American Bird Conservation Initiative (NABCI)

- Important Bird Areas (IBAs)

- Ducks Unlimited Canada projects

- North American Waterfowl Management Plan

## **3. Existing Information on Bird and Wind Turbine Interactions**

With a few important exceptions, studies that have been completed to date show very low numbers of bird fatalities at wind energy facilities. The observed mortality caused by wind energy facilities is also very low compared to other existing sources of human-caused avian mortality.  However, disturbance effects may be significant especially in offshore situations and in prairie grouse habitat.

Erickson _et al._ (2001) provide an excellent review of studies conducted across the U.S.A., evaluating how wind turbines compare to other sources of bird mortality, such as communication towers and transmission wires. Erickson _et al._ (2001) estimate an average of 2.19 bird fatalities per wind turbine per year in the U.S.A., although this estimate does not reflect the variability in fatalities among wind energy facilities (i.e., some have reported dozens of fatalities while others have reported very few or none). However, Erickson _et al._ (2001) do recognise that sites in California have significantly more fatalities than elsewhere, and estimate the fatality rate to be lower outside of California, at approximately 1.83 fatalities per turbine per year (corrected for searcher efficiency and scavenging). Based on 15,000 American wind turbines in operation, and a mortality of 2.19 birds per turbine per year, Erickson _et al._ (2001) suggest that 33,000 birds are killed each year by wind turbines in the U.S.A., 26,600 of which are killed in California. Although this may seem to be a large number of bird deaths, the impact is relatively small compared to the millions of birds that travel through wind farms each year and the millions of birds that die due to collision with transmission lines, vehicles, buildings and communication towers; for example, it is estimated that a total of 80 million birds are killed on American roads each year (Erickson _et al._ 2001, Erickson _et al._ 2002).

Another excellent review of the available literature is provided by Kerlinger (2001). This report summarises what has been found at wind farms in North America and Europe, discussing both collision rates and disturbance studies. Kerlinger (2001) presents findings similar to Erickson _et al._ (2001), reporting that no site, with the possible exception of Altamont Pass, California has caused ecologically significant mortality in the U.S.A. or in Europe. Both onshore and offshore wind farms are included in the review, although Kerlinger (2001) identifies that relatively few avian studies have been done at offshore sites. Studies examining disturbance are sparse and inconclusive, although it is evident that, in certain situations, bird behaviour is affected by wind farms (Kerlinger 2001) just as is the case with most other developments. Further detailed reviews are presented by Crockford (1992), Colson and Associates (1995), Gill _et al._ (1996), Percival (2001) and Langston and Pullan (2002).

Wind energy facilities generally have a low impact upon bird populations, but in certain situations, mortality due to collision with wind turbines can reach levels considered high. What is considered a “high” level of mortality is subjective and will differ from person to person; however, for the purposes of this report, any mortality greater than the average of 2.19 fatalities per turbine per year for the U.S., will be considered high and levels below this number will be considered low for a wind power site. It should be noted that even numbers above 2.19 birds per turbine per year can still be considered low compared to other sources of mortality ( _e.g_ ., communication towers, roads or domestic cats).

Examining the literature, there appear to be two main factors that contribute to high avian mortality, as follows:

1. _Density of birds in the area_ . In general, there is more opportunity for birds to collide with turbines when there is an abundance of birds. Indeed, the only way to guarantee no bird deaths is to place turbines where there are no birds, which is near impossible. This is not to say, however, that high bird density necessarily translates into greater bird mortality. A direct relationship between the numbers of birds in an area and collision rates has only been documented by one study in Belgium ( Everaert 2003). Other variables, in addition to high bird abundance seem to be important in determining the number of bird fatalities at a site.

2. _Landscape features in the area_ . Landforms such as ridges, steep slopes and valleys located at wind farm sites appear to increase the degree of interaction between the turbines and birds using or moving through the area, such as Neotropical migrants and raptors. The presence of other landforms such as peninsulas can funnel diurnal bird movement, which may also affect collision rates, although this has yet to be studied. These features can combine with high bird abundance to create high collision risk. For example, the presence of ridges alone near or on a proposed wind farm site does not equal high risk of raptor mortality and neither do high raptor numbers alone. However, if there exists high numbers of raptors in an area with ridges that may concentrate the birds, this can lead to higher risk of raptor collision if the wind turbines are located too close to the ridge line.

Additionally, differences in technology have been thought to contribute to differences in numbers of bird deaths. It is often believed that newer turbines have reduced collision rates, but there is very little information that clearly shows this to be the case. Older turbine technology may increase collision risk due to faster rotation of the turbine blades, but these older turbines are not solely responsible for high bird mortality observed at sites such as Altamont Pass (Anderson _et al._ 2000). More research needs to be done in this area before firm conclusions can be drawn. Most of the information about turbine technology and its effect upon birds are speculative at this time, so we advocate the precautionary principle in these guidelines.

Although collision rates are the main focus of study in North America, the effects of disturbance may cause a greater impact to birds. Unfortunately, this is the least studied aspect of wind energy facilities’ impacts on birds, but limited information is available. Some groups of birds appear to be more sensitive to disturbance from wind energy facilities than other bird groups. In particular seabirds and prairie grouse species appear to be readily disturbed by operating wind turbines and deserve particular care in planning wind energy facilities.

As background to the issues, and to help proponents identify potential conflicts with birds at proposed sites, a review of the observed impacts of wind turbines on six groups of birds follows. The groups are: waterbirds (excluding waterfowl and shorebirds), waterfowl, shorebirds, raptors, owls, and songbirds and other landbirds. For every proposed wind energy project, certain groups of birds may be more affected than others depending on where the site is located. Once a proponent has determined what birds exist at a proposed site, the following discussion will help to identify what potential effects may exist if a wind energy facility is developed.

Many studies, reviewed below, appear to show little or no impact of wind turbines on various bird species. In some cases, this apparent lack of evidence that birds were adversely affected may be an artefact of such factors as the type and intensity of monitoring. When consulting this review to identify potential problems, proponents should always consider the individual characteristics of their site and how these characteristics may act to adversely or positively affect birds, even in ways not yet documented.
