## **3.1 Waterbirds**

This group of birds includes species that are typical of water habitats, including marine environments, lakes, rivers, and wetlands, but excludes waterfowl and shorebirds, which are discussed separately (Sections 3.2 and 3.3).

Waterbirds may interact with wind turbines when facilities are located offshore, near bodies of water or near staging areas (areas where birds gather to feed before or during migration). There is little information available regarding the effects of turbines on waterbirds, but a few existing studies are discussed below.

Very few waterbird fatalities have been reported at wind energy facilities, despite the abundance of waterbirds near some turbines. For example, studies at two wind energy sites noted the abundance of cormorants nearby with very few or no cormorant fatalities. At Blyth Harbour in the United Kingdom (UK), nine modern turbines are located in an area where a large population of Great Cormorants ( _Phalacrocorax carbo_ ) spends the winter. Although these cormorants regularly fly over the area, only one fatality was recorded in seven years of surveys (Still _et al._ 1995, Percival 2001). Large numbers of migrating Double-crested Cormorants ( _Phalacrocorax auritus_ ) regularly fly through the Buffalo Ridge wind site in Minnesota, which had up to 354 modern turbines in operation during carcass surveys (Strickland _et al._ 2000a, Johnson _et al._ 2002). No cormorant fatalities have been reported during at least six years of the wind farm’s operation (Strickland _et al._ 2000a, Johnson _et al._ 2002).

There is one exception to the low number of waterbird fatalities observed at most wind energy sites. A Belgian study performed at three shoreline locations situated near to each other (East dam with 23 small to medium sized turbines, Boudewijn canal with 14 medium sized turbines, and Schelde river with three large turbines), estimated relatively high numbers of bird deaths (Everaert 2003). The findings were based on weekly or twice weekly carcass searches, corrected for searcher efficiency, scavenging and loss of carcasses in the water. At the three sites, collision rates were estimated to be 24, 35 and 18 birds per wind turbine per year, respectively (Everaert 2003). This appeared to be driven by mortality of seasonally migrating birds through the area, and not by locally breeding terns and gulls, which were observed to frequently fly through the wind farms without

incident (Everaert 2003).

The potential disturbance effects on cormorants have not been fully evaluated, but work at Blyth Harbour showed that Great Cormorants used an alternative roost site during the wind farm’s construction, only to return when construction was completed (Percival 2001).

There is no evidence to suggest that populations of herons are adversely affected by wind turbines, although there have been a few fatalities reported at wind energy facilities. One dead Great Blue Heron was found at the Nine Canyon wind power site during the 19 searches of 37 modern turbines (Erickson _et al._ 2003b). A dead Black-crowned Night-Heron ( _Nycticorax nycticorax_ ) was found at Altamont Pass during studies there (Erickson _et al._ 2001), another Black-crowned Night-Heron was found at the Pickering, Ontario Vestas V80 (1.8MW) turbine during regular searches made between January 2001 and September 2002 (James 2003), a dead unidentified egret was noted at San Gorgonio (Anderson 2000) and a Cattle Egret ( _Bubulcus ibis_ ) was found to have collided with overhead wires at a facility in Tarifa, Spain (Marti and Barrios 1995). The greatest threat that wind facilities pose to herons is the potential disturbance to nesting colonies, if turbines are located close enough to interfere with their breeding (e.g., Bowman and Siderius 1984).

Gulls have been identified as being especially vulnerable to mortality due to wind turbines because they often fly within the height of the turbine blade sphere (Airola 1987). Despite their perceived vulnerability, very low numbers of gulls have been reported to collide with turbines, except at three sites in Belgium. At the Buffalo Ridge wind site in Minnesota, large numbers of Franklin’s Gulls ( _Larus pipixcan_ ) and Ring-billed Gulls ( _L. delawarensis_ ) pass through the area during migration. A dead Franklin's Gull was reported from Buffalo Ridge during the first two years of the wind farm’s operation (Higgins _et al._ 1996), but only one dead gull (a Herring Gull _L. argentatus_ ), was found during an intensive and systematic carcass survey program performed at 91 modern wind turbines for four subsequent years (Strickland _et al._ 2000a, Johnson _et al._ 2002). Gulls are some of the most abundant bird species found at Altamont Pass in California, but only six have been reported as collision victims: two California Gulls _L. californicus_ , and four unidentified gulls, constituting approximately 1% of the total bird fatalities recorded for the area (Erickson _et al._ 2001). The three Belgian sites mentioned above (East dam, Boudewijn canal., and Schelde river) showed high gull mortality. Most collision victims were Herring Gull _Larus argentatus_ ,  Lesser Black-backed Gull _L. fuscus_ and Black-headed Gull _L. ridibundus_ , which were all abundant at the sites (Everaert 2003). It was estimated that the chance of Herring Gulls colliding with the turbines was at the East dam 1 in 3,700 (all heights) and 1 in 2,100 (rotor height). At the larger wind turbines alongside the Boudewijn canal the estimated collision chance for Herring Gull was 1 in 2,200 (all heights) and 1 in 750 (rotor height) passing birds (Everaert 2003).

At Blyth Harbour in the UK, gulls are abundant and were noted to fly through the wind site frequently (Still _et al._ 1995). Some collisions were noted, but no adverse effect on the local gull population was evident (Still _et al._ 1995). More recent studies have shown that the chance of collision may be greatest when the gulls from the resident population engage in food piracy on nonresident gulls, when their attentions are elsewhere (Lowther 2000). There is some information available to indicate that gulls show avoidance behaviour during certain times of the year (Winkelman 1995).

There is no information about how terns are affected by wind turbines, but the absence of reports of tern collisions in the literature (e.g., Thelander and Rugge 2000) suggests that collisions are uncommon. However, concerns have been raised regarding the installation of wind farms in nearshore environments that may potentially interfere with the feeding and movements of terns, such as the endangered Roseate Tern ( _Sterna dougallii)_ (Percival 2001).

For other waterbirds, only a few fatalities have been reported. Grebes, coots and rails have been found to occasionally collide with wind turbines, but numbers recorded in the literature are very small. The greatest number found was six American Coots ( _Fulica americana_ ) out of a total of 42 fatalities at the San Gorgonio wind site in California (Erickson _et al._ 2001). Other reported fatalities include species such as Western Grebe ( _Aechmophorus occidentalis_ ), Pied-billed Grebe ( _Podilymbus podiceps_ ) and Sora ( _Porzana carolina_ ) (Erickson _et al._ 2001). At the Nine Canyon wind power site, one Virginia Rail was found during the 19 carcass searches at each of the 37 modern turbines (Erickson _et al._ 2003b). One American Coot was also reported to have collided with a turbine at the Castle River Windfarm, Alberta (W.K. Brown, pers.comm., 2003).

There are some indications that offshore wind facilities may benefit waterbirds. Turbine foundations may act as artificial reefs, and reduced human fishing activity in the area appear to, in some areas, increase fish and shellfish availability. Despite these potential benefits, there is a range of potential adverse effects that may occur at offshore wind farms, including changes in the sedimentation pattern and forage species composition (Percival 2001, Merck & Nordheim 1999). In addition, offshore turbines may cause long-term habitat loss as disturbance prevents birds from using the area. Offshore installations may also act as a barrier to seasonal and local migrations, disconnecting ecological units, such as foraging and roosting sites (Exo _et al._ 2003). These problems have the potential to cause significant impacts upon populations, but due to the infancy of offshore wind farms, these problems have yet to be documented.Given the general lack of information about the specific impacts offshore installations have upon birds, and the relative infancy of the industry, caution is required when planning all offshore developments.

Wind farms could have a greater impact on waterbirds when a significant proportion of a local resource is displaced. Potentially sensitive areas may include those close to breeding colonies, and/or linked to distribution of food supply (Percival 2001). Some species feed close to their breeding colonies while others forage over great distances. It is therefore important to look at each site individually, and assess potential impact in relation to the requirements of the species present.

In summary, no significant numbers of waterbirds have been reported as collision victims at wind energy sites, even though some sites are located in areas with substantial numbers of waterbirds found nearby. The effect of disturbance from wind turbines on waterbirds has not been a subject of study at most locations, but this may be a legitimate concern at certain sites. More research is needed to examine these potentially sublethal effects, particularly on nesting herons and other colonial waterbirds.

## **3.2 Waterfowl**

The effects of wind turbines on waterfowl (ducks, geese and swans) have been examined at many wind sites, particularly in Europe. Interactions have been examined in both freshwater and marine environments, studying the effects of wind turbines near staging areas, on migration routes and at offshore sites. In general, waterfowl appear to avoid wind turbines, although some fatalities have been reported. It appears that disturbance effects are the most important factor to consider when siting wind turbines near significant waterfowl areas. The most comprehensive study of the effect of offshore wind turbines on ducks took place at Tunø Knob in Denmark, where a small, modern tenturbine offshore wind site was constructed in an area where large numbers of Common Eider ( _Somateria mollissima_ ) and Black Scoter ( _Melanitta nigra_ ) feed. Studies examining the disturbance effects of these turbines on diving ducks found that the birds exhibited avoidance behaviour, which was accentuated in poor weather conditions (Guillemette _et al._ 1999, Tulp _et al._ 1999). Eiders generally avoided flying or landing within 100 m of the turbines and avoided flying between turbines that were spaced less than 200 m apart, preferring to fly around the outer turbines (Guillemette _et al._ 1998, Guillemette _et al._ 1999, Tulp _et al._ 1999). Apart from this behaviour, no other difference in abundance or in foraging or movement behaviour was detected.

Similar findings are presented by Larsson (1994) for a study at Nogersund in Sweden, and Dirksen _et al._ (1998) for studies conducted at Lely in the Netherlands. At Lely, four 500 kW turbines were examined and two diving duck species, Common Pochard ( _Aythya ferina_ ) and Tufted Duck ( _A. fuligula_ ), were tracked at night using radar to determine their flight behaviour around wind turbines (Dirksen _et al._ 1998). Results from this study showed that most birds avoided flying near the turbines, passing around the outer turbines rather than flying between them. This suggests that lines of turbines may act as barriers to movement and should be avoided to minimise impact on bird movement in some offshore situations (Section 4.2.2). Further evidence of this is suggested by the reaction of scoters to the Confederation Bridge in the Northumberland Strait between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island during spring and fall migration. It was found that birds were very reluctant to approach the bridge and only small numbers of scoters would cross after several failed attempts. Rather than fly under the bridge (where there is ample room to pass) the birds flew very high above it (Hicklin & Bunker-Popma 2001).

The observation of avoidance behaviour is not restricted to studies at offshore wind sites. In the Yukon, a single tower was placed along the edge of the Yukon River valley where very large numbers of waterfowl migrate, including 10% of the world’s Trumpeter Swans ( _Cygnus buccinator_ ) (Mossop 1998). No collisions of any species were recorded, but it was observed that birds avoided flying close to the turbine (Mossop 1998). At the Castle River Windfarm in Alberta, ducks were observed to dramatically increase in flight altitude when they approached the wind farm so as to avoid flying through the turbines; only one dead Blue-winged Teal ( _Anas discors_ ) was found during the 96 completed surveys (W.K. Brown, pers.comm., 2003). There appear to be very speciesspecific reactions to wind turbines, as even closely related species can have very different reactions. It has been found that Pink-footed Geese are reluctant to forage within approximately 100 m of turbines, whereas Barnacle Geese have been found to forage within 25-50 m of turbines (Larsen and Madsen 2000). At Pickering, Ontario, James (2003) observed Canada Geese walking and foraging on the grass near the base of the single large turbine present at the site.

Different species of waterfowl may also react differently to offshore turbines, making it difficult to predict potential impacts upon local populations. If a species is sensitive to turbines and will not

forage within several hundred metres of a turbine, huge areas of habitat may be lost, especially if the wind farm is large (Exo _et al._ 2003). Offshore installations may also act as a barrier to seasonal and local migrations, disconnecting ecological units such as foraging and roosting sites (Exo _et al._ 2003). There is a range of potential adverse effects that may occur at offshore wind farms, including changes in the sedimentation pattern and forage species composition (Percival 2001, Merck & Nordheim 1999). These problems have the potential to cause significant impact upon populations, but due to the infancy of offshore wind farms, they have yet to be documented. Given the general lack of information about the specific effects offshore installations have upon birds, and the relative infancy of the industry, caution is required when planning all offshore developments.

With waterfowl, it is clear that the presence of large numbers of birds near wind energy facilities does not necessarily indicate that large numbers of fatalities will occur (Erickson _et al._ 2002). At Buffalo Ridge in Minnesota, it was believed that migrating waterfowl, such as Greater Whitefronted Goose ( _Anser albifrons_ ), Snow Goose ( _Chen caerulescens_ ), Canada Goose ( _Branta canadensis_ ) and Mallard ( _Anas platyrhynchos_ ), were at risk from collision due to large numbers and movements through the wind site (Strickland _et al._ 2000a). However, only three dead waterfowl (two Mallards and one Blue-winged Teal) were found in six years of surveys (Johnson _et al._ 2002). Only three geese, all Canada Geese, have been reported killed at wind farms: one at the Stateline site on the Oregon-Washington border (Erickson _et al._ 2002), and two others at Klondike, Oregon (Johnson _et al._ 2003).

Although geese and swans are very rarely victims of collision with wind turbines, small numbers of ducks have been killed, such as those noted above. Eider fatalities were noted at Blyth Harbour in the UK, but numbers of deaths decreased over time (Still _et al._ 1995). Six Common Eider deaths were attributed to collision with turbines during the first three months of the wind farm’s operation, but only three were found in the following six months, and three more were found in the 18 months following that period (Still _et al._ 1995). Collision rates declined further during the following two years (Percival 2001). The decline in collision rates was attributed to the eiders learning to avoid the turbines (Percival 2001). Overall, the number of fatalities was very small compared to the use of the area by eiders (Percival 2001).

Fatalities of dabbling ducks have been reported at wind sites close to staging, breeding and wintering areas. Sites reporting the most fatalities are those with year-round waterfowl use, with waterfowl making up to 10% or more of the total number of fatalities. However, numbers of fatalities are still very small, especially in relation to the number of ducks that use the areas (Erickson _et al._ 2002). For example, only three duck fatalities were reported from San Gorgonio, California (Anderson 2000) despite the high use of the area by waterfowl (Erickson _et al._ 2002). As many as seven duck fatalities were reported from the Altamont Pass WRA (Erickson _et al._ 2001), but, with the exception of Buffalo Ridge (see above), other studies report no more than two fatalities during carcass surveys.

## **3.3 Shorebirds**

Shorebirds have been the focus of studies in Europe when turbines are located in coastal environments where high numbers and movements of these birds occur. At the Blyth Harbour wind site in the UK, Purple Sandpipers ( _Calidris maritima_ ) overwinter in globally significant numbers (Lowther 2000). Despite this, collisions were not a problem and the sandpipers did not seem disturbed by either the construction process or the operation of wind turbines (Lowther 2000). Studies in the Netherlands (Dirksen _et al._ 1997) and Denmark (Pedersen and Poulsen 1991) examined the effect of turbines placed near important staging areas for many species of shorebirds, and found that the birds readily avoided the turbines and were at low risk of collision. However, two dead shorebirds, a Eurasian Oystercatcher ( _Haematopus ostralegus_ ) and a Common Snipe ( _Gallinago gallinago_ ), were found at a wind energy site in a Dutch estuary (Musters _et al._ 1991).

European studies have also examined disturbance impacts of wind farms on shorebirds. Results from these studies are inconsistent; some have shown that shorebirds avoid turbines up to 500m away (Winkelman 1995), while others have shown no significant effect of turbines on shorebird distribution (Thomas 1999). It is intuitive that each species will have a different threshold for disturbance, but there may be other reasons for this observed inconsistency. For example, if there is an abundance of suitable habitat near the project site, shorebirds may be more likely to move away from the turbines. If habitat is limited, birds may not have the option of relocating and therefore will remain in close proximity to the turbines (Landscape Design Associates 2000)  This may also be true for other bird groups with specific habitat requirements.

Different species of shorebirds may also react differently to offshore and near-shore turbines, making it difficult to predict potential impacts upon local populations. Shorebirds will probably be most affected by offshore turbines acting as a barrier to seasonal and local migrations, disconnecting ecological units such as foraging and roosting sites (Exo _et al._ 2003). There is a range of potential adverse effects that may occur at offshore wind farms, including changes in the sedimentation pattern and forage species composition (Percival 2001, Merck & Nordheim 1999). Even if a wind farm is located well offshore, it may possibly have a negative effect upon shorebirds that forage along the shoreline if changes in sedimentation pattern change the composition of mud (or other substrate) along the shore, which could affect availability or abundance of food supply. These problems have the potential to cause significant impacts upon populations, but due to the infancy of offshore wind farms, they have yet to be documented. Given the general lack of information about the specific impacts offshore installations have upon birds, and the relative infancy of the industry, caution is required when planning all offshore developments.North American studies have also looked at the potential risk to shorebirds posed by wind energy projects. Several species of shorebirds were considered to have a high risk of collision during spring and fall migration at Buffalo Ridge in Minnesota, since large numbers fly through the site (Strickland _et al._ 2000a). Despite the high numbers of shorebirds passing through the site, only one shorebird carcass, that of a Killdeer ( _Charadrius vociferus_ ), was found during six years of surveys (Johnson _et al._ 2002).

The low collision rate of shorebirds may be related to their flight behaviour. Shorebirds tend to fly at high altitudes when migrating or travelling between feeding areas, and descend or ascend rapidly when approaching or leaving feeding areas. This behaviour rarely places shorebirds at blade height and may help explain the low observed numbers of collisions (Wind Power Pty Ltd. 2003). It seems

that in most areas, shorebirds are not likely to collide with turbines. However, turbines placed in close proximity to large numbers of staging shorebirds should be avoided. Shorebirds are easily disturbed by predators and people, and this potentially creates a situation where large numbers could collide with turbines as they try to escape a real or perceived threat. Siting away from significant staging areas of shorebirds, particularly in coastal environments, may be an important element to consider.

## **3.4 Diurnal Raptors**

Diurnal raptors found in Canada include eagles, buteos, accipiters, Northern Harrier, Osprey and falcons. Turkey Vultures are also included within this group due to their similarity to many soaring raptors with respect to flight behaviour and habitat use, although taxonomically New World vultures are more closely related to storks.

Raptor collisions with wind turbines in the Altamont Pass and Tehachapi Pass areas in California are the main cause of concern regarding the effects of wind turbines on birds. These sites contain thousands of turbines, making them some of the largest in North America. In 1989, the California Energy Commission issued a report that reviewed data on bird collisions with wind turbines in this state between 1984 and 1988 (California Energy Commission 1989). A total of 108 individuals of seven species were found, most of which were raptors protected by both California and U.S. law. Most of the collisions were recorded during winter when large numbers of raptors occupy the area while hunting for mammalian prey.

To address these findings a two-year study was undertaken by BioSystems Analysis Inc. (Orloff and Flannery 1992). Observations and mortality searches were conducted for six seasons examining a sample of approximately 16% of the 7000 turbines at Altamont. Of the 183 dead birds found during this study, 119 (65%) were raptors, the majority of which were Red-tailed Hawks ( _Buteo jamaicensis)_ , American Kestrels ( _Falco sparverius)_ , and Golden Eagles ( _Aquila chrysaetos)_ . In total, approximately 55% of all raptor deaths were attributed to turbine collision, 8% to electrocution, 11% to wire collision, and 26% could not be determined (Orloff and Flannery 1992). Several factors were proposed as posing the greatest risk to raptors: end-row turbines, turbines within 500 m of a canyon and turbines with a lattice-type tower (Orloff and Flannery 1992). High raptor mortality in the Altamont Pass area continues to be seen. Between 1998 and 2000, 256 dead birds were found, 139 (54.3%) of which were raptors (Erickson _et al._ 2002, Hunt 2002).

Since these initial studies in California, there have been many more studies dealing with this issue both in the Altamont Pass area and at other wind turbine sites. Raptors have been the focus of many studies for several reasons:

- there is a relatively high proportion of raptors killed at some wind energy sites;

- • raptors have a high public profile;

- some raptor species have relatively small populations and/or slow breeding rates, such that any increase in mortality may have a significant negative effect realised at the population level; and,

- raptors often fly at heights within the blade sweep area and may be vulnerable to wind turbine collisions.

Another wind energy site that has had significant raptor mortality is in Tarifa, Spain. This site is on the edge of the Strait of Gibraltar and forms a “bottleneck” that concentrates bird migration in the Mediterranean basin. Soaring birds are generally of greatest concern, since at least 30,000 individual raptors and huge numbers of storks pass through the area in the autumn. The raptors and storks that pass through Tarifa comprise a large proportion of the populations that nest in Western Europe and winter in Africa. The most common soaring species that pass through the area include the Honey Buzzard ( _Pernis apivorus_ ), Black Kite ( _Milvus migrans_ ), and White Stork ( _Ciconia ciconia_ ), but many non-soaring species also migrate through the area (Marti 1995).

The Tarifa area has been internationally recognised as an “Important Bird Area” by Bird Life International, has been declared a “Special Protection Area” by the European Union and is a Natural Park as designated by the Andalusian government (Marti 1995). There are several wind facilities in the area with a total of 268 older wind turbines in operation (Marti 1995). Some of these facilities are aligned roughly parallel to the main migration direction, but some turbine strings cross the migration pathway at an angle. Thousands of soaring birds land and roost on the ground or promontories in the area, including areas with wind turbines. Many collisions with the turbines have been recorded, including those of 14 protected species. A total of 106 individuals were estimated to have been killed over the span of one year, 49 of which were Common Kestrels ( _Falco tinnunculus_ ) and 30 were Griffon Vultures ( _Gyps fulvus_ ) (Marti and Barrios 1995). Almost all recorded deaths occurred on days with high visibility (Marti and Barrios 1995).

There have been very few raptor fatalities reported at wind sites other than Altamount and Tarifa. In the U.S.A. outside of California, raptors comprise only 2.7% of turbine-related deaths (Erickson _et al._ 2001), or a total of 6 individual raptors (Kerlinger 2001). The low numbers of fatalities observed at most wind sites is most likely due to better siting of turbines (away from problem topography and high raptor concentrations). It has been speculated that the construction of tubular (as opposed to lattice-type) towers and slower blade speeds may also have helped to lower raptor fatalities, but studies that have examined mortality levels at different types of turbines have shown no significant difference between technologies (Anderson _et al._ 2000).

The most important factor that influences raptor collisions appears to be topography. A good example exists when comparing Tehachapi Pass, and the San Gorgonio Pass Wind Resource Areas (WRA). Tehachapi Pass is located in south-central California at elevations of 1000-1600m above sea level. It contains many ridges and slopes and approximately 5,000 turbines of various makes and sizes. San Gorgonio Pass is a narrow, low elevation pass situated 180-850m above sea level in California, containing 3,750 turbines, also of various makes and sizes. At each site, 830 carcass searches occurred over one year and it was found that raptor mortalities where much higher at Tehachapi Pass (8 Red-tailed Hawks, 1 Ferruginous Hawk _Buteo regalis_ , 1 unidentified buteo, 7 American Kestrels, and 1 Prairie Falcon _Falco mexicanus_ ) than at San Gorgonio Pass (1 Red-tailed Hawk) (Anderson _et al._ 2000). Therefore, it appears that landform features such as elevation, ridges and slopes are very important in determining the amount of raptor mortality in areas where raptors

## are abundant.

In most areas, raptors appear to have little trouble avoiding the turbines when simply flying or soaring even when at blade height. Osborn _et al._ (1998) found that during 20 months of monitoring, no American Kestrel was found dead although they were commonly observed flying at blade height and within 15m of the turbines. Numerous other studies, including those conducted in Canada, have also shown low raptor collision numbers. At the Castle River Windfarm in Alberta, Red-tailed Hawks and American Kestrels were numerous yet only one raptor collision, that of a kestrel, was observed during the 96 carcass surveys done over two years of study (W.K. Brown, pers.comm., 2003).

It is easy to dismiss Altamont and the few other problem locations as not being relevant to new wind energy projects because of the special combination of topography and high densities of birds, but they should not be ignored. They provide important examples of problems that should be avoided when siting future wind energy facilities. Wind turbine/raptor interactions will not be an issue in most areas, but site selection processes and EAs should consider topographical features and areas of high raptor density, with preference for siting facilities away from high risk areas so as to avoid the potential for raptor collision.

## **3.5 Owls**

There is little or no information about how owl species react to turbines, but owls typically fly within turbine height or lower, which may put them at risk of collision. Examining the species composition of fatalities, owls are included in the lists of collision victims at a number of sites. The numbers of owls killed at each site varies, representing a proportion at some sites of up to 10-15% of the total numbers of birds killed. As examples, 69 owls were killed at Altamont Pass, comprising 11.3% of total fatalities (number derived from several studies examining up to 1169 <250kW turbines done between 1988 and 1998); five (11.9%) were killed at the San Gorgonio wind site (quarterly searches were made at ~360 <250kW turbines between 3/97 to 5/98), and 18 (12.2%) were found at Tehachapi Pass (quarterly searches were made at 640-760 <250kW turbines between 5/95 and 5/98) (Erickson _et al._ 2001). However, many sites report far fewer owl fatalities, and many record none at all (e.g., Osborn _et al._ 2000).

## **3.6 Landbirds**

Amongst the landbirds, songbirds (passerines) comprise the bird group most commonly affected by wind energy facilities in North America, outside of California. Although disturbance and habitat loss associated with turbine construction are adverse effects, songbird fatalities due to turbine collision have attracted the most attention in studies. Protected songbirds (under SARA or MBCA) comprise 78% of all fatalities documented at wind energy sites in the U.S.A. (Erickson _et al._ 2001). This proportion would be even higher if it included legislatively unprotected i.e., nonnative species such as European Starling ( _Sturnus vulgaris_ ) and House Sparrow ( _Passer domesticus_ ). In comparison, raptors comprise only 2.7% of all turbine-related fatalities in the U.S.A.

The number of songbird fatalities varies considerably between sites, and often there is little or no

relationship between the numbers of birds moving through an area and the numbers of birds found dead as a result of turbine strikes. For example, the Buffalo Ridge wind site in Minnesota is located in an area where large numbers of birds move through during migration; using radar, as many as 3.5 million birds are estimated to pass over the wind development area each year (Johnson _et al._ 2002). Despite the large numbers of birds moving through, collision rates are low. During the first two years, a total of 73 turbines were in operation, and an average of 0.49 collisions per turbine per year was recorded. The site was then expanded, and 354 modern turbines were monitored from 1996 to 1999. The new collision rate was calculated to be 2.85 fatalities per turbine per year (Johnson _et al._ 2002), with a conservative estimate of 1009 birds killed annually at the site, which was corrected for scavenging and searcher efficiency. Elsewhere, very few or no dead songbirds have been found despite being located in areas with an abundance of both breeding and migrating songbirds (Erickson _et al._ 2001, Kerlinger 2001). One study performed in Belgium shows a positive linear relationship between the number of bird flights through a wind farm and the number of the collisions observed (Everaert 2003). Although examining only large gulls passing through the wind farm, the report that more collisions are found with increases in bird flights is interesting (Everaert 2003).Although songbirds are the most abundant victims of turbine collision, numbers can still be considered very small when compared to the total number of songbirds that use most wind farm areas. No study has yet demonstrated that turbines have significantly affected a songbird population. However, recent declines in Neotropical migrant bird populations on both their breeding and wintering grounds have been cause for concern. Habitat alteration and destruction is likely the major threat to these birds, but large numbers are killed by obstructions along their migration routes. Communication towers, lighted skyscrapers, vehicles, communication wires, houses and roads all take their toll to varying degrees. Therefore, it is important to minimise the impact that wind farms might have upon migrating bird populations, especially of Neotropical migrants.

Many songbirds migrate at night (particularly Neotropical migrants), and typically fly at altitudes of 150m or higher, above the maximum height of most wind turbines. During this night-time migration, birds tend to fly in broad fronts over water and land, although large topographical features (e.g., mountains and high ridges) can concentrate birds along relatively narrow pathways. During the day, most birds tend to stay within 20-30m of the ground (within or near vegetation) to avoid predation and to rest and feed. Many nocturnal migrants will continue to migrate for at least part of the day, but will do so at these lower altitudes. On a typical day during migration, birds move between higher and lower altitudes at dawn and dusk, and it is during these times that nocturnal migrants may be at risk of colliding with wind farm structures (Richardson 2000, Langston and Pullan 2002).

Although nocturnal migration typically occurs at heights above most wind farm structures, collisions still occur, even with structures lower than 100m in height; a few examples of mass collision events with low structures are given below (see Avery 1980 for a complete summary). On October 7, 1954 about 1000 birds (22 species) were found on a parking lot at Oak Ridge, Tennessee (Dunbar 1954). Birds had collided with overhead power lines, light towers, cars, and pavement, with most carcasses found beneath the parking lot lights (Dunbar 1954). Lights also appeared to be a factor in the collision of 144 birds (30 species) with a brightly lit ski lift in Gatlinburg between September 21 and 22, 1963 (Savage 1963). However, lights are not always a factor in mass kills at

low structures. For example, Wylie (1977) found 73 dead birds of 21 species at a fire tower in West Virginia, following a night of fog and rain. The 30m Sand Springs Fire Tower sits atop Chestnut Ridge, approximately 800m in elevation. The tower is not lit and no lights occur anywhere in that part of the Cooper’s Rock State Forest, in which it is located. In this example, inclement weather and siting on a ridge at a high elevation contributed to the risk of collision even with an unlit and relatively short structure.

A few multiple bird collision events have occurred at wind farms, although none have yet come close to the numbers killed at communication towers. The largest was 27 birds at the Mountaineer site in West Virginia on a foggy night in late May 2003. The birds were found at three turbines and a brightly lit substation. It appears that the sodium vapour lights at the substation attracted the migrants and was the main cause of the collisions, as there were many other turbines that were lit with red strobe lights (12 of a total of 44 turbines at the site) and no fatalities were found at these turbines, only the ones adjacent to the substation (Kerlinger 2003). It should be noted that, although there was only one multiple collision event, a total of an additional 28 night migrants were found during the year (a total of 65 fatalities of 21 species). When corrected for searcher efficiency and scavenging a total of 180 birds were killed a year at 44 turbines (4 birds/turbine/year)(Kerlinger 2003), which is a high number for a wind farm.

Another example of a multiple bird collision event also occurred during a period of inclement weather during spring migration. A combined total of 14 birds collided with two unlit wind turbines at Buffalo Ridge, Minnesota, on the night of May 16/17, 1999 (Johnson _et al._ 2002). Elsewhere, an estimated total of 170 birds were killed at 18 wind turbines at Oosterbierum, Netherlands, during seven consecutive nights in the fall of 1988 (Winkelman 1995). A third example of multiple bird kills occurred at a wind turbine in Nasudden, Sweden, where 43 birds were found dead near one turbine during very poor weather conditions; the turbine was not operational at the time, but was lit with a single lamp 10m above the ground (Gill _et al._ 1996). Overall, mortality events of this magnitude are seldom recorded and continue to be a rare phenomenon, but can occur during periods of poor weather.

Inclement weather can increase the risk of bird collision with wind farm structures. For example, clouds have an influence on the altitude of migrants by forcing higher flying migrants to lower altitudes, which increases the density of migrants near the ground and increases the probability of collisions with tall obstacles. A cloud ceiling that drops to near or below the height of the turbines will affect high altitude migration, inducing migrants to move at or below treetop level (Robbins 2002). Drizzle and fog impair visibility and also cause birds to fly at lower altitudes, to follow topographical clues. Combined with lighting that may attract migrating birds, migrants may collide with turbines, other wind farm structures (including guyed anemometers), or each other, or they may circle the structures until exhausted, falling to the ground where they are at risk of dying due to exposure or predation. If there is a high proportion of fog days during migration at the project site, there may be an increased risk of collision.

As mentioned earlier, the greatest threat to Neotropical migrant songbirds is habitat loss and destruction. The impact of turbines on forest nesting birds has only been examined once in North America, during a short-term study at Searsburg, Vermont (Kerlinger 2003b). It was found that

disturbance to most birds was low, with several species nesting in the forest within 20-30m of the turbines. A few species were, however, found to avoid the clearing where the turbines were located and some appeared to move further into the forest (notably Swainson’s Thrush). It is unclear whether this movement was related to avoidance of the turbines or the clearing (Kerlinger 2003b). It is clear that there is a need for further study to determine how wind turbines may affect forest nesting birds.

In general, there is very little detailed information about the effects of wind energy developments on other groups of landbirds. Most information pertains to carcasses of a few species in amongst other casualties, and no detailed study has looked at sublethal effects of wind farms, such as disturbance of breeding species, with the possible exception of grassland grouse species (see below).

Doves and pigeons appear to be susceptible to collisions with turbines. The non-native and legislatively unprotected Rock Pigeon ( _Columba livia_ ) is often the most commonly killed species at wind farms. At the San Gorgonio WRA in California, ten Rock Pigeons were killed during one study, making up 23.8% of the total number of bird fatalities (quarterly searches were made at ~360 <250kW turbines between 3/97 to 5/98) (Erickson _et al._ 2001). At Altamont Pass during the many years of study, a total of 92 Rock Pigeons fatally collided with the turbines, making up 15% of the total fatalities recorded (number derived from several studies examining up to 1169 <250kW turbines done between 1988 and 1998) (Erickson _et al._ 2001). Dove mortality was also observed at the Castle River Windfarm, Alberta. Here, one Rock Pigeon and two Mourning Doves ( _Zenaida macroura_ ), the latter protected under the MBCA, were found during 96 carcass surveys (W.K. Brown, pers. comm., 2003). Considering the affinity of Rock Pigeons for human structures and settlements, the number of fatalities may not be surprising. Overall, fewer Mourning Doves have been found killed, although they are still regularly recorded as victims, comprising between less than 1% of the total numbers of birds killed to a high of 4.1% (six individuals) at Tehachapi Pass, California (quarterly searches were made at 640-760 <250kW turbines between 5/95 and 5/98) (Erickson _et al._ 2001). Unfortunately these studies did not report on the total number of doves using these sites, making it difficult to put the mortality observed in perspective.

Woodpeckers have been recorded as collision victims only a few times. One Northern Flicker ( _Colaptes auratus_ ) was killed at Montezuma Hills, three Northern Flickers were killed at Tehachapi Pass, one Northern Flicker was killed at Castle River, one Lewis’s Woodpecker ( _Melanerpes lewis_ ) was found dead at a wind farm at Vansycle, Oregon, and one Yellow-bellied Sapsucker ( _Sphyrapicus varius_ ) fatality was recorded at a Wisconsin site (Erickson _et al._ 2001, W.K. Brown, pers. comm., 2003). These species usually fly below the blade sweep and are not typically at risk of collision.

There may be greater collision risk to bird species with aerial courtship displays such as Horned Lark, Vesper Sparrow and Bobolink. These species are known to fly high enough at times during these displays to potentially collide with turbines and they are frequent collision victims at western wind energy sites where these birds are very common (Kerlinger & Dowdell 2003). At the Nine Canyon wind power project in Washington,  Horned Larks comprised 47% (17 individuals) of all collision victims found during 19 searches conducted over a year at each of the 37 1.3-MW turbines and one un-guyed meteorological tower (Erickson _et al._ 2003b).  Horned Larks are also the most common fatality at the Stateline wind project, which is located close to the Nine Canyon project

(Erickson _et al._ 2003). The greater risk to these birds will generally not be a concern in areas where they are common, but this issue should be taken seriously in areas such as BC where the local subspecies of the Horned Lark is considered Endangered.

In addition to increased collision risk to these species it has been shown that turbines may displace many (but not all) grassland species. Leddy _et al_ . (1999) found that there were fewer nesting  grassland birds within 100-200 metres of turbines in southwestern Minnesota. Densities decreased by more than 50% in the area within approximately 50 m of turbines. It remains unknown if nesting grassland birds will become habituated to turbines and return to areas from where they were previously displaced. Not all grassland species are displaced by turbines: at the Ponnequin Wind Energy Facility in Colorado, grassland songbirds like Horned Larks forage directly beneath turbines and Western Meadowlarks were also found to forage directly beneath turbines at Altamont in California (Curry & Kerlinger, LLC studies in progress, cited in Kerlinger 2003b).

Upland gamebirds are at low risk of collision with turbines as they generally fly below the blade sweep, but collisions have been known to occur. Between 1996 and 1999, 354 turbines were surveyed at the Buffalo Ridge wind site in Minnesota. Out of a total of 55 dead birds, three were gamebirds (one Gray Partridge _Perdix perdix_ and two Ring-necked Pheasants _Phasianus colchicus_ ). At Tehachapi Pass in California, four Chukar ( _Alectoris chukar_ ) and three California Quail ( _Callipepla californica_ ) were found killed by wind turbines (Erickson _et al._ 2001). Two Ringnecked Pheasants were also found during 19 carcass searches of 37 modern wind turbines at the Nine Canyon wind power project (Erickson _et al._ 2003b). Risk of collision appears to be nonsignificant, but sublethal effects, such as disturbance, must be considered for some of the more sensitive species.

Probably the greatest potential threat that wind facilities pose to game birds is habitat destruction, fragmentation and disturbance of local breeding populations. Of particular concern are threats to prairie grouse (Sage Grouse _Centrocercus urophasianus_ and Sharp-tailed Grouse _Tympanuchus phasianellus_ ). Prairie grouse and other ground-dwelling grassland species have been shown to be very vulnerable to human changes in the landscape, and to avoid any elevated structure (e.g., trees, power poles) as raptors (their predators) often use them as perches. It has been shown that Lesser Prairie-Chickens ( _T. pallidicinctus_ ) will not nest or brood within 400m of a road or 300m from power lines, and will also avoid areas that have humans present, such as inhabited dwellings (Manes _et al._ 2002). Due to their strong avoidance of tall structures, prairie grouse could abandon extensive areas around wind turbines despite the presence of otherwise suitable habitat.

Prairie grouse species require large expanses of contiguous suitable habitat, such as short grass, mixed grass and sage brush prairie. Humans have long influenced grasslands and over 90% of the native prairie has been eliminated by agricultural land use (Manes _et al._ 2002). The result is that populations of many grassland species are rapidly declining in North America, which makes remaining habitat very important to the survival of these sensitive species. Much of this remaining suitable habitat is located in remote areas or where topography makes agriculture difficult. However, some of these sites may have suitable wind resources, and there is the potential for wind facilities to be constructed in these ecologically ‘healthy’ and pristine locations. Introducing wind turbines and other structures to these sites can adversely affect already sensitive and vulnerable grassland species. To help alleviate negative effects on grassland birds, wind energy facilities should be sited on land that has already been altered (e.g., cultivated cropland) and away from high quality prairie habitat.

## **4. Potential Sources of Avian Impact for a Wind Energy Project**

Below are descriptions of several key aspects of wind energy developments that have the potential to cause adverse environmental effects. This list should not be considered exhaustive, but rather the minimum to be considered when assessing environmental effects on wintering, breeding and migrating birds.

## **4.1 Scale of Facility**

## **4.1.1  Onshore Facilities**

The scale of the facility can impact the amount of bird mortality and disturbance. Simply put, under comparable conditions, a large facility has the potential to affect more birds than a small one. Table 1 presents information on the number of carcasses reported at a number of wind farms in the U.S.A., in relation to their size (i.e., number of turbines sampled). The total wind farm size is not presented in the table as mortality is unknown at turbines not sampled and extrapolation is avoided. What the table shows is that, in general, more sampled turbines equate to more observed fatalities. This can then be used to see that more dead birds will be found at a site as the number of turbines (or number sampled) increases. Numbers of carcasses were not corrected for searcher efficiency or carcass removal (via scavenging or any other means), but the data show that there is a trend for more turbines to kill more birds in a year even if numbers are underestimated. This does not necessarily mean that more turbines kill _disproportionately_ more birds per year, on a per turbine basis, but it does show simply that more turbines will result in more avian collisions and more bird deaths.

A small wind farm is not likely to kill a large number of birds. Table 1 shows that many wind farms where up to 30 turbines were sampled report fewer casualties than this, but nevertheless, it is unlikely that even 22 birds killed at a wind farm each year would be considered a significant impact, unless some of those fatalities were of Species at Risk. However, a larger facility with more than 100 turbines may kill many more birds, approaching or exceeding levels that officials may deem unacceptable. The number and siting opportunities of wind farms in an area should also be considered. It would, for example, be better to have one very large wind farm in one well sited location instead of many small poorly sited ones. As such, it is important to consider both the average effect of each turbine and the cumulative effect of the total number of turbines in the area.
